inspection_summary: The article outlines a conditional completeness argument for the 3-primes problem by joining three scale-specific components: a GRH-based asymptotic theorem above 10^20, a GRH-based nearby-prime lemma below that threshold, and a finite Goldbach verification for the resulting even differences. Its most reusable content is the explicit interface between analytic positivity, interval control for primes, and a set-covering computation, together with comparisons explaining the chosen estimates and computational representation.

sections_inspected.label: Front matter and abstract
sections_inspected.mathematical_role: Identifies the conditional theorem and previews its asymptotic, intermediate, and computational components.

sections_inspected.label: Introduction
sections_inspected.mathematical_role: Defines the 3-primes problem, contrasts unconditional and GRH-dependent numerical thresholds, states the result, and gives the three-part proof architecture.

sections_inspected.label: The asymptotic theorem
sections_inspected.mathematical_role: Reduces representation to positivity of a weighted counting function and outlines a refined major-arc/remainder decomposition under GRH.

sections_inspected.label: An intermediate lemma
sections_inspected.mathematical_role: Uses an explicit GRH estimate for the Chebyshev theta function to locate a prime whose subtraction leaves a bounded even difference, and compares a nominally sharper alternative estimate.

sections_inspected.label: The computer search for 2-primes representations
sections_inspected.mathematical_role: Connects the nearby-prime lemma to a finite Goldbach theorem and describes two covering algorithms, the optimized prime representation, primality certification inputs, bit-array implementation, and reported exhaustive range.

accepted_units.title: GRH changes an unreachable finite remainder into a computable one
accepted_units.why_material: The introduction contrasts unconditional bounds that leave an infeasible residual range with GRH-based refinements and computation, then states the complete conditional theorem. This supplies the numerical-design motivation for the paper's hybrid proof rather than merely historical background.
accepted_units.context_note: The span includes the problem definition, the comparison of prior thresholds, the proposed combination of methods, and the theorem statement.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Numerical exponents are visibly degraded by PDF spacing, but the comparative role of the bounds and the theorem statement are recoverable from the prose.

accepted_units.title: Three-part analytic-to-computational decomposition
accepted_units.why_material: The proof is factored into an asymptotic theorem, a nearby-prime lemma, and a two-prime computation; this is the source's central modular interface and explains how the conditional conclusion is assembled.
accepted_units.context_note: This concise roadmap is self-contained and is developed by the next three sections.

accepted_units.title: Weighted representation count turns existence into a positivity comparison
accepted_units.why_material: The source encodes prime triples with von Mangoldt weights, expresses the count through a truncated integral, and reduces existence to proving that a leading term dominates an explicitly bounded remainder above 10^20.
accepted_units.context_note: The span includes the asymptotic theorem, definitions of the representation count and exponential sum, and the stated positivity plan; it does not include the subsequent arc construction.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Several displayed formulas are degraded by extraction, so exact notation requires scan verification; the prose still clearly supports the weighted-count, integral, and leading-term-versus-remainder mechanism.

accepted_units.title: Narrowed major arcs isolate a GRH-controlled remainder
accepted_units.why_material: The main analytic refinement is to shrink the major-arc intervals, split the integral into a leading part and a complementary remainder, and use a GRH zero-sum estimate for the exponential sum on that remainder.
accepted_units.context_note: The interval definitions, parameters, remainder lemma, and the stated Hardy-Littlewood treatment of the leading term are kept together because severing them would obscure what was refined and what the lemma controls.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Exact interval endpoints, set decorations, and the bound on S(a) are formula-sensitive and partly garbled; scan verification is needed for transcription, while the structural split is explicit in the prose.

accepted_units.title: A theta-function error bound produces a nearby prime and a bounded even remainder
accepted_units.why_material: Under GRH, a bound for the Chebyshev theta function rules out an excessively long prime-free interval and yields a prime p for which n-p lies between 4 and 1.615 times 10^12. This is the analytic bridge that compresses every remaining odd case into the range of the two-prime computation.
accepted_units.context_note: The lemma statement and its contradiction-style estimate are retained as one unit; the next lines separately compare the chosen estimate with an alternative.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: The summation and inequality typography is degraded, including the theta glyph and constants; the lemma's inputs, conclusion, and prime-gap argument are recoverable from the checked prose, but exact formulas require scan verification.

accepted_units.title: A better asymptotic log factor can lose to a smaller explicit constant
accepted_units.why_material: The authors explain that a GRH estimate with one log factor was not used because its derived constant made it numerically worse at the operative scale than Schoenfeld's two-log estimate. This is a reusable warning that finite-range optimization can reverse an asymptotic preference.
accepted_units.context_note: This note directly qualifies the estimate used in the preceding lemma.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: The theta notation is mistranscribed, but the comparison in prose is clear.

accepted_units.title: Subtracting the nearby prime reduces the residual task to finite Goldbach verification
accepted_units.why_material: The source explicitly composes the intermediate lemma with the theorem that every even number through 10^13 is a sum of two primes: for an odd n below 10^20, n-p is even and small enough for the verified range.
accepted_units.context_note: The extracted inequality in line 179 loses a comparison sign, so the upper bound is read together with the immediately preceding lemma rather than reconstructed externally.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Line 179 is extraction-defective, but lines 177-182 and the preceding source lemma make the parity-and-range bridge recoverable; exact typography should be checked against the scan.

accepted_units.title: Conventional Goldbach verification as cumulative translated-set coverage
accepted_units.why_material: The usual computation builds primes in a target interval and cumulatively unions their translations by small odd primes until every even target is covered. The passage isolates prime generation as the bottleneck and records how the auxiliary interval margin depends on the largest small prime used.
accepted_units.context_note: Definitions and the reported prior-work scale are included to make the set-cover interpretation coherent.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Extracted calligraphic set names are inconsistent, but the recurrence and coverage criterion are recoverable from prose and displayed structure.

accepted_units.title: Search near the interval endpoint and precompute the small difference primes
accepted_units.why_material: The optimized approach reverses which prime set is expensive: it takes consecutive primes near the interval start, precomputes odd primes only up to roughly the interval width, and covers targets by translated copies of that fixed small-prime set. A density calculation motivates a finite candidate count without serving as the certification itself.
accepted_units.context_note: The span includes the new recurrence, fixed interval width, size estimate, and heuristic explaining the choice of candidate count.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Set symbols and superscripts are degraded, and the density calculation is heuristic; the algorithmic reversal is explicit in prose.

accepted_units.title: The optimized covering method trades one reusable sieve for cheap per-interval prime discovery
accepted_units.why_material: The paper directly compares resource profiles: the older method sieves all primes in every high interval, while the new method sieves a larger low prime table once and then locates only a bounded list of primes near each interval. It also states the semantic cost: the witness prime is not extremal.
accepted_units.context_note: This is the cost-and-output comparison following the construction and empirical choice of k.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Numerical powers have spacing artifacts, but the one-time-versus-per-interval tradeoff is clear.

accepted_units.title: Bounded-base strong-pseudoprime tests certify the needed nearby primes
accepted_units.why_material: The generation of primes near each interval start relies on quoted size thresholds under which passing strong-pseudoprime tests to specified initial prime bases implies primality, turning a probabilistic-looking filter into a bounded deterministic certificate for this range.
accepted_units.context_note: The unit reports the exact certification dependency as stated; it does not independently verify the cited result.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: The integer thresholds and bases are legible in the normalized text, though scan verification remains prudent for exact numerical reuse.

accepted_units.title: Bitset shifts realize coverage and the completed range is reported with a worst witness
accepted_units.why_material: Each small-prime translate is implemented as an OR with a shifted primality bit array, making set coverage vectorizable. The authors report exhaustive coverage from 4 times 10^11 through 10^13, timing evidence, and the largest observed number of nearby-prime trials, which together describe both certification scope and workload behavior.
accepted_units.context_note: The implementation, covered range, costs, and extremal reported case are retained together as the source's computational evidence statement.
accepted_units.representation_dependency: Bit semantics and reported coverage are clear; exact large integers and powers should be scan-checked before machine reuse because of PDF extraction spacing.

within_source_synthesis_candidates.title: Scale-bridging conditional completeness
within_source_synthesis_candidates.claim: The source composes analytic positivity above a threshold with a nearby-prime reduction below it and formally bounded exhaustive two-prime coverage, so each component is responsible for a distinct numerical scale and interface.
within_source_synthesis_candidates.limit: The argument is conditional on GRH, the asymptotic proof is only outlined, and the computational verification is reported rather than reproduced in this article.

within_source_synthesis_candidates.title: Finite-scale constants govern the analytic-computational boundary
within_source_synthesis_candidates.claim: The useful analytic estimate is selected by its explicit finite-range constant, because that constant determines the maximum even remainder that the computational theorem must cover.
within_source_synthesis_candidates.limit: The normalized formulas are extraction-sensitive and the numerical comparison is tied to the stated scale near 10^20.

within_source_synthesis_candidates.title: Goldbach verification as translated-set coverage
within_source_synthesis_candidates.claim: Reframing witness search as cumulative coverage by translated prime sets exposes a data-layout choice: precompute the reusable small-difference primes, cheaply generate a few high primes per interval, and realize each translation as a bitset shift and OR.
within_source_synthesis_candidates.limit: The density argument only motivates the candidate count; completeness comes from actual interval coverage, and primality generation depends on the quoted bounded-base result.
